question.prompt: When one ounce of water is added to a mixture of acid and water, the new mixture is \(20\%\) acid. When one ounce of acid is added to the new mixture, the result is \(33\frac13\%\) acid. The percentage of acid in the original mixture is

solutions.explanation:
After the water is added, \(20\%=1/5\) of the mixture is acid, so the acid-to-water ratio is \(1:4\). After the acid is added, \(33\frac13\%=1/3\) is acid, so that ratio becomes \(1:2\).

The amount of water stays unchanged during the second addition. Relative to this same amount of water, the acid increases from one-fourth as much to one-half as much, so its amount doubles. The increase is one ounce, which means there was one ounce of acid before that addition. There were therefore four ounces of water at that stage.

Removing the one ounce of water added in the first step leaves the original mixture with one ounce of acid and three ounces of water. Its acid percentage was
\[
\frac{1}{1+3}\cdot100\%=\boxed{25\%},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Track the unchanged water

solutions.explanation:
Let \(u\) be the total number of ounces immediately after adding the water. Since the original mixture has positive total amount, \(u>1\). At this stage the acid amount is \(u/5\) ounces.

Adding one ounce of acid makes the total \(u+1\) ounces and the acid amount \(u/5+1\) ounces. The final acid fraction is \(1/3\), so
\[
\frac{u}{5}+1=\frac{u+1}{3}.
\]
Multiplying by \(15\) gives
\[
3u+15=5u+5,
\]
so \(u=5\). Thus the acid amount was one ounce, and the original total was \(5-1=4\) ounces. The original acid percentage was
\[
\frac14\cdot100\%=\boxed{25\%},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\). These amounts also give two ounces of acid in six ounces after both additions, as required.
solutions.title: Model the total after adding water
